title: Set Theory & Venn Diagrams
summary: Sets, subsets and Venn diagrams: two- and three-group survey counting shared by SSC, Railway, Banking and CAT papers. A handful of formulas — union, inclusion–exclusion and max–min bounds — solve nearly every question. Most errors come from misreading regions, not from hard algebra.

subtopics.title: Sets, Subsets & Power Sets
subtopics.concept: A set is a well-defined collection of objects, and Venn diagrams are its picture. The core skill here is counting: subsets, unions, intersections and complements. Most exam questions are direct formula applications.

formulas.name: Number of subsets
formulas.note: A set with $n$ elements; the power set has $2^n$ elements.

formulas.name: Proper subsets
formulas.note: All subsets except the set itself.

formulas.name: Non-empty subsets
formulas.note: All subsets except the empty set.

formulas.name: Non-empty proper subsets
formulas.note: Drops both the empty set and the full set.

formulas.name: Subsets of size r
formulas.note: Order does not matter inside a subset.

formulas.name: Union of two sets
formulas.tex: n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)
formulas.note: Subtract the overlap counted twice.

formulas.name: De Morgan's laws
formulas.tex: (A \cup B)' = A' \cap B',\quad (A \cap B)' = A' \cup B'
formulas.note: A complement swaps the join sign.

tricks.title: Know powers of 2 by heart
tricks.body: Subset questions are pure powers of two. Learn $2, 4, 8, \ldots, 512$ and every variant (proper, non-empty) becomes a one-step subtraction.

example.q: A set has 9 elements. How many subsets does it have?

tricks.title: Count what you do not want
tricks.body: For 'at least one of these elements' or 'non-empty proper', count the unwanted subsets and subtract from $2^n$.

example.q: A set has 6 elements. How many non-empty proper subsets does it have?
steps: Drop the empty and the full set: $64 - 2 = 62$.

tricks.title: De Morgan turns the question into one union
tricks.body: $n(A' \cap B')$ looks scary. De Morgan converts it to $n(U) - n(A \cup B)$, a two-line count.

example.q: In a universal set of 80 elements, $n(A) = 45$, $n(B) = 35$ and $n(A \cap B) = 15$. Find $n(A' \cap B')$.

mistakes: Using $2^n$ where a smaller count is asked — proper subsets are $2^n - 1$ and non-empty proper subsets are $2^n - 2$.
Adding $n(A)$ and $n(B)$ without subtracting the overlap — the common elements get counted twice.
Reading $n(A - B)$ as $n(A) - n(B)$ — subtract the overlap $n(A \cap B)$, not the whole of $n(B)$.
Mixing up De Morgan — $(A \cup B)'$ becomes $A' \cap B'$, not $A' \cup B'$.
Forgetting the empty set when listing subsets — $\emptyset$ is a subset of every set.
Treating equivalent sets as equal — equal needs the same elements; equivalent only the same count.
subtopics.notes:
### What a set is
A set is a collection of well-defined objects. The objects are called its elements.

Write a set in roster form: $A = \{2, 4, 6, 8\}$. Then $n(A) = 4$, the number of elements.

- $4 \in A$ means 4 belongs to A.
- $5 \notin A$ means 5 does not belong to A.

Two sets are **equal** when they have exactly the same elements. They are **equivalent** when they only have the same number of elements. $\{1, 2\}$ and $\{3, 4\}$ are equivalent but not equal.

The empty set $\emptyset$ has no elements, so $n(\emptyset) = 0$. A singleton set has exactly one element.

### Subsets and the power set
$A$ is a subset of $B$ (written $A \subseteq B$) when every element of A is also in B.

Each element makes two choices: in or out. So a set with $n$ elements has $2^n$ subsets.

The set of all subsets is the **power set**. A power set of an $n$-element set has $2^n$ elements.

- Subsets: $2^n$
- Proper subsets (drop the set itself): $2^n - 1$
- Non-empty subsets (drop the empty set): $2^n - 1$
- Non-empty proper subsets: $2^n - 2$

> **Rule:** For $n$ elements: subsets $2^n$, proper $2^n - 1$, non-empty proper $2^n - 2$.

Check with $A = \{1, 2, 3\}$: the 8 subsets are $\emptyset$, three singletons, three pairs and the full set. Proper: 7. Non-empty proper: 6.

### Subsets of a fixed size
Subsets with exactly $r$ elements are counted by $^{n}C_r$.

From $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$, the subsets of size 2 number $^{6}C_2 = \dfrac{6 \times 5}{2} = 15$.

To count subsets that must contain a given element, put that element in first and choose the rest from the remaining $n - 1$. To count subsets that must avoid an element, choose everything from the other $n - 1$.

> **Tip:** "At least one of two given elements" flips to "avoid both". Count the avoid case and subtract from $2^n$.

### Union, intersection, difference, complement
Take $A = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ and $B = \{3, 4, 5\}$.

- Union $A \cup B = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$, so $n(A \cup B) = 5$: in A or B or both.
- Intersection $A \cap B = \{3, 4\}$, so $n(A \cap B) = 2$: in both.
- Difference $A - B = \{1, 2\}$: in A but not in B.
- Complement $A' = U - A$: everything of the universal set $U$ outside A.

> **Rule:** $n(A - B) = n(A) - n(A \cap B)$. Subtract the overlap, not $n(B)$.

### The union counting formula
$$n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$$

Adding $n(A)$ and $n(B)$ counts the common elements twice. Subtract the overlap once.

Worked: $n(A) = 23$, $n(B) = 18$, $n(A \cap B) = 9$. Union $= 23 + 18 - 9 = 32$.

The formula also runs backwards. If the union is known, any one of the other three counts follows from it.

> **Tip:** "At least one of A or B" always means the union. Spot those words and reach for this formula.

### De Morgan's laws
The complement flips unions and intersections:

$$(A \cup B)' = A' \cap B' \qquad (A \cap B)' = A' \cup B'$$

In words: "not in A or B" means "outside A and outside B".

Exam use: $n(A' \cap B') = n(U) - n(A \cup B)$.

Worked: $n(U) = 50$, $n(A) = 30$, $n(B) = 24$, $n(A \cap B) = 10$. Union $= 44$, so $n(A' \cap B') = 50 - 44 = 6$.

> **Watch:** A complement turns $\cup$ into $\cap$ and $\cap$ into $\cup$. Do not keep the same join sign.

patterns.name: Number of subsets of a set
patterns.howToSpot: 'How many subsets does a set with n elements have?' — a direct power-set ask.
patterns.why: Each element independently joins or stays out, so the choices double for every element.

example.q: A set has 6 elements. How many subsets does it have?

patterns.name: Proper and non-empty subsets
patterns.howToSpot: The word 'proper' (drop the set itself) or 'non-empty' (drop the empty set) is attached to subsets.
patterns.why: Proper removes the full set and non-empty removes the empty set from the $2^n$ total.

example.q: A set has 5 elements. How many non-empty proper subsets does it have?

patterns.name: Subsets of a fixed size or containing given elements
patterns.howToSpot: 'Exactly 2 elements', 'containing a particular element', or 'at least one of two given elements'.
steps: Must contain a set of k elements: choose the rest from $n - k$.
At least one of some elements: $2^n$ minus the subsets avoiding all of them.
patterns.why: Fixing or banning elements just shrinks the pool that the remaining choice works on.

example.q: A set has 6 elements. How many subsets have exactly 2 elements?

patterns.name: Union of two sets and the difference region
patterns.howToSpot: $n(A \cup B)$ or $n(A - B)$ is asked from counts of $A$, $B$ and $A \cap B$.
patterns.formula: n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B);\quad n(A - B) = n(A) - n(A \cap B)
steps: Write the union formula (or the difference formula).
Subtract the overlap for a union; subtract it from $n(A)$ for a difference.
patterns.why: The plain sum double-counts the overlap, so it must be removed once.

example.q: If $n(A) = 21$, $n(B) = 17$ and $n(A \cap B) = 8$, find $n(A \cup B)$.

patterns.name: De Morgan complement count
patterns.howToSpot: The ask uses complements like $n(A' \cap B')$ or words like 'outside both A and B'.
steps: Convert the complement expression with De Morgan.
patterns.why: 'Not (A or B)' equals 'not A and not B', so the complement of the union is the answer.

example.q: In a universal set of 50 elements, $n(A) = 30$, $n(B) = 24$ and $n(A \cap B) = 10$. Find $n(A' \cap B')$.

revision: Subsets of an $n$-element set: $2^n$; power set has $2^n$ elements.
De Morgan: $(A \cup B)' = A' \cap B'$, $(A \cap B)' = A' \cup B'$.

subtopics.title: Two-Set Venn Diagrams
subtopics.concept: Two overlapping circles inside a rectangle give four regions. Every two-group question is a read-off from those regions once the overlap is found. One formula, $n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$, does most of the work.

formulas.name: Union
formulas.tex: n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)
formulas.note: At least one of the two groups.

formulas.name: Only A
formulas.note: The wing region outside B.

formulas.name: Exactly one
formulas.note: Only A plus only B.

formulas.name: Neither
formulas.note: Outside both circles.

tricks.title: Fill the four regions, then read off
tricks.body: Get the overlap first, then peel off each wing. Every ask — both, only, exactly one — becomes a subtraction.

example.q: In a class of 100 students, 60 take History, 55 take Geography and 20 take neither. How many take both subjects?

tricks.title: Four regions must add to the total
tricks.body: Only A $+$ only B $+$ both $+$ neither $=$ total. Use it as a check, or to find the one missing region.

example.q: In a survey of 150 people, 85 like tea, 80 like coffee and 30 like both. How many like neither?

tricks.title: Exactly one subtracts the overlap twice
tricks.body: At least one is the union; exactly one removes the overlap from it. One subtraction apart.

example.q: In a group of 100 people, 60 like tea, 55 like coffee and 25 like both. How many like exactly one drink?

mistakes: Putting 'neither' inside the circles — neither $= n(U) - n(A \cup B)$ and sits outside both.
Reporting $n(A) - n(A \cap B)$ as 'both' — that is only A; both is $n(A \cap B)$ itself.
Using $n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$ for exactly one — subtract the overlap twice.
Answering the union when 'exactly one' is asked — at least one and exactly one differ by the overlap.
Dropping one region in the final check — the four regions must add exactly to the total.
Forgetting that 'every person likes at least one' fixes the union at the group size.
subtopics.notes:
### The picture: two circles in a box
Draw two overlapping circles inside a rectangle. The rectangle is the universal set.

The four regions are: only A, only B, both, and neither. Their counts always add to the total.

Worked: a class of 60 has 35 tea drinkers and 30 coffee drinkers, and 10 drink neither.

1. At least one drink: $60 - 10 = 50$.
2. Both: $35 + 30 - 50 = 15$.
3. Only tea: $35 - 15 = 20$; only coffee: $30 - 15 = 15$.
4. Check: $20 + 15 + 15 + 10 = 60$.

> **Rule:** only A $= n(A) - n(A \cap B)$. Get the overlap first; every other region follows.

### The union formula
$$n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$$

"Tea or coffee" means at least one of the two. The plain sum counts the overlap twice, so subtract it once.

The formula runs backwards too: $n(A \cap B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cup B)$.

When every person belongs to at least one group, the union is the whole group size.

Worked: an office of 90 employees has 55 Hindi speakers and 40 English speakers, and everyone speaks at least one. Both $= 55 + 40 - 90 = 5$.

> **Example:** A class of 70 has 45 chess players and 40 card players, with 10 playing neither. The union is $60$, so both $= 45 + 40 - 60 = 25$.

### The neither region
"Neither" sits outside both circles. Count the union first, then subtract from the total.

$$\text{neither} = n(U) - n(A \cup B)$$

Worked: 90 people, 50 like cricket, 45 like football, 25 like both. Union $= 50 + 45 - 25 = 70$, so neither $= 90 - 70 = 20$.

> **Tip:** "At least one" and "neither" always add to the total. They are complements.

### Exactly one
"Exactly one" counts the two wing regions only.

$$\text{exactly one} = n(A) + n(B) - 2\,n(A \cap B)$$

Worked: 200 people, 120 read paper A, 90 read B, 45 read both. Exactly one $= 210 - 90 = 120$.

> **Watch:** "At least one" subtracts the overlap once; "exactly one" subtracts it twice.

### Reading the words carefully
The wording decides the region.

- "like A or B" — usually the union.
- "like A or B but not both" — exactly one.
- "do not like either" — neither.
- "only A" — the wing region.

Underline the deciding words before computing. One word changes the answer.

Compare two asks on the same data: 60 people, 35 speak Hindi, 30 speak English, everyone speaks at least one.

- "How many speak both?" gives $35 + 30 - 60 = 5$.
- "How many speak only Hindi?" gives $35 - 5 = 30$.

> **Note:** Options in the exam usually include the union answer for an exactly-one question. Read twice, then answer.

### Ratio problems on four regions
When a region is a multiple of another, name the smaller one $x$.

Worked: a class of 45, everyone plays cricket or badminton, only-cricket is twice only-badminton, and 9 play both.

1. Let only badminton $= x$; only cricket $= 2x$.
2. $x + 2x + 9 = 45$, so $x = 12$.
3. Badminton players $= 12 + 9 = 21$.

> **Note:** The four-region sum is one linear equation. Ratios only fix the coefficients.

patterns.name: Find both from totals and neither
patterns.howToSpot: Two group sizes, the total, and a 'neither' line; the overlap is asked.
patterns.formula: n(A \cap B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cup B)
steps: Check the four regions add to the total.
patterns.why: Removing the neither block first makes the union the sum the formula needs.

example.q: In a group of 120 people, 70 like tea and 65 like coffee. If 15 like neither, how many like both?

patterns.name: Find neither from totals and both
patterns.howToSpot: Group sizes and the overlap are given; 'how many like none' is asked.
steps: Keep the neither block outside the circles.
patterns.why: The union covers everyone in a circle, so the total minus it is exactly the outside block.

example.q: In a survey of 90 people, 50 like cricket and 45 like football, and 25 like both. How many like neither?

patterns.name: Only-A / only-B regions
patterns.howToSpot: 'Only tea', 'only Hindi', 'have a bicycle but not a scooter' — a single wing region is asked.
steps: Subtract it from the group size.
patterns.why: The overlap is the part of the circle shared with the other, so removing it leaves the pure wing.

example.q: In a class of 100 students, 60 take History, 55 take Geography and 20 take neither. How many take only History?

patterns.name: Exactly one of the two
patterns.howToSpot: 'Exactly one', 'but not both', or 'one of the two only' appears in the question.
steps: Or subtract $2 \times$ both from the plain sum.
patterns.why: Exactly one keeps the wings and drops the shared middle completely.

example.q: In a group of 300 people, 180 speak Hindi, 150 speak English and 60 speak both. How many speak exactly one language?

patterns.name: Total when everyone is covered
patterns.howToSpot: 'Every person plays at least one' with the group size asked.
patterns.why: With no outside block, the total and the union are the same number.

example.q: Every student of a class studies at least one of Hindi or English. 18 study Hindi, 14 study English and 6 study both. How many students are in the class?

patterns.name: Ratio between the wing regions
patterns.howToSpot: 'Only cricket is twice only badminton' — one region is a multiple of another.
steps: Write the four-region sum with the multiples of $x$.
Add the overlap back for the full group size if asked.
patterns.why: The four regions add to the total, so the ratio turns it into one linear equation.

example.q: In a class of 48 students, every student plays at least one of cricket or badminton. The number playing only cricket is twice the number playing only badminton. If 9 play both, how many play badminton?

revision: Four regions add to the total: wings $+$ both $+$ neither $= n(U)$.
'Every person at least one' means the union is the whole total.

subtopics.title: Three-Set Venn Diagrams
subtopics.concept: Three overlapping circles create seven regions inside the union. The union formula adds the singles, subtracts the pairs and adds back the triple. Word problems hide one region and give the rest.

formulas.name: Union of three sets
formulas.tex: n(A \cup B \cup C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - p_{AB} - p_{BC} - p_{CA} + t
formulas.note: $p$ are the pair intersections and $t$ the triple.

formulas.name: Exactly two
formulas.note: Petals only; the triple is removed from each pair.

formulas.name: At least two
formulas.note: Exactly two plus the triple.

formulas.name: Exactly one
formulas.note: The three wings together.

tricks.title: Add singles, subtract pairs, add the triple
tricks.body: One line gives the union. Sing the sign pattern $+ + +\ -\ -\ -\ +$ while writing it.

example.q: For three sets, $n(A) = 22$, $n(B) = 18$, $n(C) = 16$, $n(A \cap B) = 7$, $n(B \cap C) = 5$, $n(A \cap C) = 6$ and $n(A \cap B \cap C) = 2$. Find $n(A \cup B \cup C)$.

tricks.title: Exactly two: pair sum minus three times the triple
tricks.body: Each pair count hides the triple. Subtract it three times to strip it out of all three pairs.

example.q: Pair counts are 16, 12 and 10, and 5 elements lie in all three sets. How many lie in exactly two sets?

tricks.title: Exactly one: singles minus twice the pairs plus three times the triple
tricks.body: The wings survive only after both double and triple counting is removed.

example.q: $n(A) = 24$, $n(B) = 20$, $n(C) = 16$, $n(A \cap B) = 8$, $n(B \cap C) = 6$, $n(A \cap C) = 7$, $n(A \cap B \cap C) = 2$. How many elements lie in exactly one set?

mistakes: Subtracting the triple the wrong number of times — the union formula adds it back once after the pairs are subtracted.
Using pair sums directly as 'exactly two' — subtract $3t$ for exactly two and $2t$ for at least two.
Forgetting that 'at least two' includes the all-three region.
Adding the singles and calling it the union — every overlap must be removed first.
Leaving a negative region in the diagram — a negative count means the data is inconsistent.
Mixing 'exactly one' with 'at least one' — they differ by every multi-set region.
subtopics.notes:
### The union formula for three sets
$$n(A \cup B \cup C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - n(A \cap B) - n(B \cap C) - n(A \cap C) + n(A \cap B \cap C)$$

Say it as: add singles, subtract pairs, add back the triple.

Why: a point in exactly two sets is counted twice by the singles, so subtract one copy. A point in all three is counted three times by the singles and three times removed by the pairs — so add one copy back.

Worked: $n(A) = 30$, $n(B) = 25$, $n(C) = 20$; pairs $10, 8, 9$; triple $4$.

Union $= 75 - 27 + 4 = 52$.

> **Rule:** The signs run $+, +, +, -, -, -, +$ in that order. Write them before substituting.

### The seven regions
Three circles cut the union into seven regions: three "only" wings, three "exactly two" petals and one middle.

Fill the regions in this order:

1. Start from the middle: the triple count.
2. Each petal: pair count minus the triple.
3. Each wing: single minus its two petals minus the triple.

Worked: pairs $10, 8, 9$, triple $4$: petals are $6, 4, 5$.

> **Tip:** Fill all seven regions once and every sub-question becomes a read-off.

### Exactly two and at least two
Pair sums count the triple region three times — once inside each pair.

$$\text{exactly two} = (p_{AB} + p_{BC} + p_{CA}) - 3t$$
$$\text{at least two} = (p_{AB} + p_{BC} + p_{CA}) - 2t$$

Worked: pairs $16, 14, 12$, triple $6$. Exactly two $= 42 - 18 = 24$; at least two $= 42 - 12 = 30$.

Exactly two and the triple cannot overlap, so at least two is just their sum: $24 + 6 = 30$.

### Exactly one
$$\text{exactly one} = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - 2(p_{AB} + p_{BC} + p_{CA}) + 3t$$

Worked: singles $26, 22, 18$; pairs $9, 7, 5$; triple $2$.

Exactly one $= 66 - 42 + 6 = 30$.

> **Watch:** 'At least two' includes the triple; 'exactly two' does not. One word changes the coefficient.

### Solving backwards
Word problems usually hide the triple. Put $t$ in the formula and solve.

Worked: union $70$; singles $42, 36, 30$; pairs $18, 14, 12$.

$70 = 108 - 44 + t$, so $t = 6$.

When "none" is mentioned, first write union $= $ total $-$ none, then solve for $t$.

> **Note:** "Every person likes at least one" means the union equals the total. That sentence is often the key equation.

### The sanity check
No region can be negative. Compute the wings; a negative wing means the data is impossible.

Each wing: $n(A) - p_{AB} - p_{CA} + t$. If this drops below zero, the given numbers cannot all be true.

Options that force a negative region are wrong choices, not answers.

> **Watch:** Before trusting any answer, check all seven regions are non-negative and add to the union.

patterns.name: Union of three sets
patterns.howToSpot: Three singles, three pairs and a triple are given; 'at least one' is asked.
patterns.formula: n(A \cup B \cup C) = \Sigma\,n(A) - \Sigma\,n(A \cap B) + n(A \cap B \cap C)
patterns.why: Each overlap is removed as many times as it was counted in excess.

example.q: For three sets, $n(A) = 25$, $n(B) = 20$, $n(C) = 15$, $n(A \cap B) = 8$, $n(B \cap C) = 6$, $n(A \cap C) = 5$ and $n(A \cap B \cap C) = 3$. Find $n(A \cup B \cup C)$.

patterns.name: Reverse-solve the triple intersection
patterns.howToSpot: The union (or 'everyone covered') is known, and $n(A \cap B \cap C)$ is asked.
steps: Move every known count to one side.
patterns.why: The union equation is linear in $t$, so one known union pins it down.

example.q: $n(A \cup B \cup C) = 55$ with $n(A) = 32$, $n(B) = 28$, $n(C) = 24$, $n(A \cap B) = 12$, $n(B \cap C) = 9$ and $n(A \cap C) = 10$. Find $n(A \cap B \cap C)$.

patterns.name: Exactly two regions
patterns.howToSpot: 'Exactly two' with three groups — the petals of the diagram are asked.
patterns.why: Each pair sum includes the triple once, so stripping the triple needs three subtractions.

example.q: In a group, 45 like tea, 40 like coffee and 35 like milk. 18 like tea and coffee, 12 like coffee and milk, 15 like tea and milk, and 5 like all three. How many like exactly two drinks?

patterns.name: Exactly one region
patterns.howToSpot: 'Exactly one' with three groups — the wings of the diagram are asked.
patterns.why: A wing element is counted once, a petal twice and the middle three times by the singles.

example.q: $n(A) = 35$, $n(B) = 30$, $n(C) = 25$, $n(A \cap B) = 12$, $n(B \cap C) = 10$, $n(A \cap C) = 8$ and $n(A \cap B \cap C) = 3$. How many elements lie in exactly one set?

patterns.name: At least two regions
patterns.howToSpot: 'At least two' or 'two or more' with three groups.
steps: Or add exactly two and the triple.
patterns.why: The triple is inside every pair, so two of its three copies must be removed.

example.q: In a group, 45 like tea, 40 like coffee and 35 like milk; 20 like tea and coffee, 15 like coffee and milk, 12 like tea and milk, and 5 like all three. How many like at least two drinks?

patterns.name: None of the three
patterns.howToSpot: 'How many play none / like neither of the three' with a fixed total.
steps: Check the union does not exceed the total.
patterns.why: The union covers everyone inside a circle, so the leftover is the outside block.

example.q: In a class of 75 students, 40 play cricket, 35 play hockey and 30 play football. 15 play cricket and hockey, 12 play hockey and football, 10 play cricket and football, and 3 play all three. How many play none?

revision: Fill seven regions once; read every answer off.
A negative region means inconsistent data.

subtopics.title: Maximum–Minimum Region Problems
subtopics.concept: When totals are fixed, regions cannot take any size they like. Maximum and minimum questions ask for the extreme possible size of one region. Two bounds decide everything: the union cannot exceed the total, and no region can be negative.

formulas.name: Maximum overlap
formulas.note: One set wholly inside the other.

formulas.name: Minimum overlap
formulas.note: $N$ is the size of the universal set.

formulas.name: Maximum neither
formulas.note: Shrink the union to its largest member set.

formulas.name: Minimum triple
formulas.note: Union fixed at $N$; everyone covered.

formulas.name: Maximum triple
formulas.note: All three sets nested.

tricks.title: Push the smaller set inside the larger
tricks.body: For a maximum overlap, nest the circles. The smaller group sits entirely inside the bigger one.

example.q: In a class of 45 students, 28 play cricket and 22 play football. What is the maximum number who play both?

tricks.title: Min overlap: stretch the union to its limit
tricks.body: Let the two circles cover as many people as the total allows. The forced sharing is the answer.

example.q: In a group of 80 people, 50 like tea and 45 like coffee. What is the minimum number who like both?

tricks.title: Leftover demand forces the triple
tricks.body: Singles beyond $2N$ cannot fit outside the middle. Subtract $2N$ from the singles sum.

example.q: In a group of 120 people where everyone likes at least one drink, 110 like tea, 90 like coffee and 80 like milk. What is the minimum number who like all three?

mistakes: Calling $n(A) + n(B) - N$ the maximum overlap — that is the minimum when the total is fixed.
Allowing a negative minimum — write $\max(0,\ n(A) + n(B) - N)$; counts cannot go below zero.
Comparing with the wrong total — the bound uses the universe size, not the sum of the groups.
Assuming the minimum overlap is always 0 — with a tight total it is forced above zero.
Maximising 'neither' by shrinking both circles — only the largest set must stay whole.
Skipping the achievability check — every Venn region must stay non-negative at your extreme.
subtopics.notes:
### Two bounds run everything
Region sizes cannot wander freely. Two rules bind them:

1. The union never exceeds the total: $n(A \cup B) \le N$.
2. No region is negative.

Maximum questions push a region up; minimum questions push it down. Apply the two rules and the extremes fall out.

### Maximum overlap of two sets
One circle can sit wholly inside the other.

$$\max n(A \cap B) = \min(n(A), n(B))$$

Worked: 120 like cricket and 100 like football in a group of 200. Maximum both $= 100$ — every football lover also likes cricket.

### Minimum overlap of two sets
Stretch the union to its largest, $N$. The overlap is then squeezed to its smallest.

$$\min n(A \cap B) = \max\left(0,\ n(A) + n(B) - N\right)$$

Worked: in a group of 100, 60 drink tea and 50 drink coffee. Minimum both $= 60 + 50 - 100 = 10$.

> **Rule:** If $n(A) + n(B) > N$, at least $n(A) + n(B) - N$ people must sit in both. Counts cannot be negative, so keep the floor at 0.

### Maximum 'neither' and minimum union
"Neither" is largest when the union is smallest, and the union cannot drop below its largest member set.

$$\max \text{neither} = N - \max(n(A), n(B))$$

Worked: 50 students, 30 like maths and 25 like physics. Maximum neither $= 50 - 30 = 20$: everyone who likes physics also likes maths.

The same bound gives the minimum union of three sets: it is the largest of the three counts.

### Three sets and the triple
The same two bounds fix the triple's limits.

- Maximum triple $= \min(n(A), n(B), n(C))$.
- Minimum triple $= \max\left(0,\ n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - 2N\right)$.

Why the minimum: a person outside the triple sits in at most two of the three sets. The singles total can therefore hide at most $2N$ memberships outside the middle, and whatever is left over must sit in all three.

Worked: everyone in a group of 150 likes at least one of tea (120), coffee (110) and milk (100). Minimum triple $= 330 - 300 = 30$.

> **Watch:** The formula needs the union fixed at $N$. If people may like none, replace $N$ by the number who like at least one.

### Extremes of the derived regions
Exactly one and at least two move opposite to the overlap.

- Exactly one is smallest when "both" is largest: $n(A) + n(B) - 2\min(n(A), n(B))$.
- For three sets, at least two $= n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - n(A \cup B \cup C) - t$, so it is smallest when the triple $t$ is largest.

Worked: 130 play cricket and 120 play football in a group of 200. Both can reach 120, so exactly one can drop to $250 - 240 = 10$.

> **Note:** After computing an extreme, check every region stays non-negative. If some region breaks, the extreme is not achievable.

mistakes: Mixing counts and percentages in one equation — convert everything to one scale first.

Forgetting the triple sits inside every pair sum when solving a percentage caselet.

subtopics.notes:
### Turn sentences into regions
A survey caselet is a set question wearing words. Underline each group name and each joining word.

- "like tea" — a single count.
- "like tea and coffee" — the overlap.
- "like none of these" — the neither block.

Write the four-region sum and fill what is given. The one unknown region falls out of the total.

Worked: a survey of 250 students has 130 taking Mathematics and 120 taking Biology, while 40 take neither.

1. At least one subject: $250 - 40 = 210$.
2. Both: $130 + 120 - 210 = 40$.
3. Check: only Maths $90$ $+$ only Biology $80$ $+$ both $40$ $+$ neither $40$ $= 250$.

### Percentage surveys
Work on a base of 100 when everything is in percent. The arithmetic is the same; only the units change.

Worked: 65% read A, 48% read B, 20% read neither.

1. At least one $= 80\%$.
2. Both $= 65 + 48 - 80 = 33\%$.
3. Exactly one $= 80 - 33 = 47\%$.

When a percent must become people, multiply it by the survey total.

> **Tip:** Never mix counts and percents in one line. Convert everything to one scale first.

### Surveys with three groups
Languages and three-product surveys use the three-set union formula. Keep a small table: three singles, three pairs, the triple and none.

Worked: 55% tea, 45% coffee, 35% milk; pairs 18%, 15%, 12%; triple 6%.

Union $= 135 - 45 + 6 = 96\%$, so none $= 4\%$.

> **Note:** With "every person likes at least one", the union must equal 100%. That pins a hidden triple.

### Checking the data
Real surveys sometimes carry impossible numbers. Regions catch them.

- The union cannot exceed the total.
- Each "only" region must stay non-negative.

Worked: 200 people; singles 120, 100, 90; pairs 60, 50, 45; triple 30.

Union $= 310 - 155 + 30 = 185$, so none $= 15$. A report claiming "no one said none" would be wrong.

> **Watch:** If a region turns negative, do not force an answer — the data is inconsistent.

### CAT-style caselets
A caselet gives four or five facts and asks two or three sub-questions. The hidden unknown is usually the triple intersection.

1. Write the union formula with $t$ for the triple.
2. Use "everyone covered" or the total to fix the union.
3. Solve for $t$, then fill all seven regions.
4. Answer each sub-question by reading the regions.

Worked: 60% tea, 50% coffee, 45% milk; pairs 25%, 20%, 15%; everyone drinks at least one.

1. Union $= 155 - 60 + t = 95 + t$.
2. The union must be $100\%$, so $t = 5\%$.
3. Every sub-question is now a read-off: only tea $= 25\%$, both tea and coffee only $= 20\%$.

> **Tip:** Percentages multiply cleanly on a base of 100. Keep the base fixed through the whole caselet.

By De Morgan, $A' \cap B' = (A \cup B)'$.

Set A has one element more than set B, and set A has 64 more subsets than set B. How many elements does A have?
practice.solution:
Let B have $m$ elements. Then $2^{m+1} - 2^m = 64$, so $2^m = 64$ and $m = 6$.
A has $6 + 1 = 7$ elements.
practice.shortcut: One extra element doubles the subsets: the extra count is itself $2^m$.

practice.q: In a universal set of 100 elements, $n(A) = 55$, $n(B) = 45$ and $n(A' \cup B') = 70$. Find $n(A \cap B)$.
practice.solution:
By De Morgan, $A' \cup B' = (A \cap B)'$.
So $n(A \cap B) = 100 - 70 = 30$.
practice.shortcut: The complement flips the join: 'outside A or outside B' is 'not in both'.

practice.q: A set has 9 elements. How many of its subsets contain at least one of two particular given elements?
practice.solution:
Subsets avoiding both given elements: $2^{9-2} = 2^7 = 128$.
Required $= 2^9 - 2^7 = 512 - 128 = 384$.
practice.shortcut: Complement counting: count what you do not want and subtract from $2^n$.

Singles sum $= 195$, so extra memberships $= 195 - 130 = 65$.
At least two $= 65 - t$, so maximise the triple $t$.
$t \le (195 - 130) \div 2 = 32$ (exactly-two regions cannot go negative).
Minimum $= 65 - 32 = 33$.
practice.shortcut: Each 'at least two' person absorbs extra memberships; push the triple as high as it can go.

practice.q: In a survey of 400 people, 240 watch news channels, 200 watch movies and 100 watch both. How many people watch neither?
In a group of 250 students, 130 opted for Mathematics, 120 opted for Biology and 40 opted for neither. How many students opted for both?
In a town, 55% of families have a television and 45% have a refrigerator. If 25% have neither, what percentage of families have both?
In a class of 70 students, 40 like tea, 35 like coffee and 15 like both. How many students like exactly one drink?
Of 300 employees in a company, 180 know Hindi and 150 know English. If 60 know neither language, how many know exactly one language?
practice.solution:
At least one $= 240$. Both $= 330 - 240 = 90$.
Exactly one $= 240 - 90 = 150$.

practice.q: In a survey of 500 households, 310 own a smartphone, 260 own a laptop and 90 own neither. How many households own both?
In a survey, 65% of the people read newspaper A, 48% read newspaper B and 20% read neither. What percentage read exactly one newspaper?
In a group of 600 people, 75% speak Hindi and 40% speak English, and 10% speak neither language. How many people speak both languages?

In a college, 40% of students play cricket, 30% play football and 20% play hockey. 10% play cricket and football, 8% play football and hockey, 6% play cricket and hockey, and 2% play all three. What percentage of students play none of the games?

In a survey of 200 people, 120 like tea, 100 like coffee and 90 like milk. 60 like tea and coffee, 50 like coffee and milk, 45 like tea and milk, and 30 like all three. How many people like none of the three drinks?
In a class of 80 students, every student plays at least one of two games. 50 play chess and 55 play cards. How many students play chess only?

In a hostel, 60% of students drink tea, 50% drink coffee and 45% drink milk. 25% drink tea and coffee, 20% drink coffee and milk and 15% drink tea and milk. Every student drinks at least one beverage. What is the minimum percentage of students who drink all three?
practice.solution:
Union $= (60 + 50 + 45) - (25 + 20 + 15) + t = 95 + t$.
Everyone drinks at least one, so the union is $100\%$: $95 + t = 100$.
$t = 5\%$.
practice.shortcut: With the union pinned at 100%, the triple is fixed, not free.
